question.text: An eigenvector of $D = \left[\begin{array}{cc} -8&10\\-7&11 \end{array}\right]$ corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda=6$ is $\left[\begin{array}{c} c \\ 14 \end{array}\right].$ Determine the value of $c.$
question.explanation:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $D$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $D\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} D\mathbf{v} &= \lambda \mathbf{v} \\[5pt] \left[ \begin{array}{cc} -8 & 10\\ -7 & 11 \end{array}\right] \left[ \begin{array}{cc} c \\ 14 \end{array}\right] &= 6 \left[ \begin{array}{cc} c \\ 14 \end{array}\right] \\[5pt] \left[ \begin{array}{c} -8c+140\\ -7c+154 \end{array} \right] &= \left[ \begin{array}{c} 6c \\ 84 \end{array}\right] . \end{align*}

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

\[ \begin{cases} -8c+140=6c\\ -7c+154=84 \end{cases} \]

  • Solving for $c$ in the first equation, we get \[ -8c+140=6c \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c = 10. \]

  • Solving for $c$ in the second equation, we get \[ -7c+154=84 \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad c = 10. \]

Therefore, the solution of the system is $c=10.$

question.text: The eigenvector of $A = \left[\begin{array}{cc} -3&1\\3k+1&3 \end{array}\right]$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-k$ is $\left[\begin{array}{c} 1 \\ 5 \end{array}\right].$ Determine the value of $k.$
question.explanation:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ So, we have

\begin{align*} A\mathbf{v} &= \lambda \mathbf{v} \\[5pt] \left[ \begin{array}{cc} -3& 1\\ 3k+1 & 3 \end{array}\right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} 1\\ 5 \end{array} \right] &=-k\left[ \begin{array}{c} 1\\ 5 \end{array} \right] \\[5pt] \left[ \begin{array}{cc} 2\\ 3k+16 \end{array}\right] &= \left[ \begin{array}{c} -k\\ -5k \end{array}\right] . \end{align*}

This gives us the following system of linear equations:

\[ \begin{cases} 2=-k,\\ 3k+16=-5k \end{cases} \] Solving for $k$ in the first equation, we get \[ 2=-k \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad k = -2. \]

Now, substituting $k=-2$ into the second equation, we get \begin{align*} 3k +16 &=-5k \\[5pt] 3\cdot (-2)+16 &= -5\cdot (-2) \\[5pt] 10 &= 10, \end{align*} which is a true statement.

Therefore, the solution of the system is $k=-2.$

question.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. If $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{3}$ then $\mathbf{v}$ is also an eigenvector of the matrix $A^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda=4.$
  2. An eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ is also an eigenvector of the inverse $A^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$
  3. If $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=3,$ then $5\mathbf{v}$ is also an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda=15.$
question.explanation:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $\mathbf{v}$ such that $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda \mathbf{v}.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

  • Statement is false. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have \[ A\mathbf{v} = \dfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{v}. \] Multiplying it by $A^{−1}$ from the left, we obtain \[ \mathbf{v} = \dfrac{1}{3} A^{-1}\mathbf{v}. \] Multiplying both sides by $3$, we get \[ A^{-1}\mathbf{v}= 3\mathbf{v}. \] So, $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $3.$

Note: In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ is an eigenvector of $A^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\dfrac{1}{\lambda}.$

  • Statement II is true. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$ is an eigenvector of $A^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda=-\dfrac{1}{2}.$

  • Statement III is false. We have \begin{align*} A(5\mathbf{v}) = 5 A\mathbf{v} = 5 (3 \mathbf{v}) = 3(5 \mathbf{v} ). \end{align*} Since, $A(5\mathbf{v})=3( 5 \mathbf{v} ),$ and $5 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0},$ this implies that $5 \mathbf{v} $ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda = 3.$

Note: In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."
